spec.title: The decision memo with a number in it
spec.intro:
You own one control area, and this lab ends with the artifact that proves it: a
build-vs-buy decision memo a finance partner would accept. Your workspace is the lab
directory — the committed FAIR-style fixture (`risk-input.json`, the §5.2 scenario:
12 standing prod-db grants that never expire), the reference calculator's source
(`expected_loss.ts`, read it — it is ~80 lines), a scoring-table skeleton, and the
memo template. The **Run validator** button runs the module's own calculator against
`risk-input.json`: the same deterministic TypeScript the lab ships, ported line for
line and CI-verified byte-identical to real `bun expected_loss.ts` runs — every
number you see here is the real tool's output, not a prop. On your own machine the
same flow is `bash labs/setup.sh`, then `bun expected_loss.ts fixtures/risk-input.json`.
One honesty note: the checks here are structural — they verify the memo has every
load-bearing part, not that your judgment is good. The judgment is the part that
transfers, and it is yours.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 1 — the product card. In the memo's **Control as a product** section, pick
one real control you own (or keep the §5 prod-db access control) and complete the
card in the §5.1 shape: `Owner:` exactly one accountable human (a name — not a team,
not a committee), `Customers (priority order):` at least two of engineer/auditor/
business as a numbered list in deliberate order, `Backlog (ranked):` your top three
defects numbered with the riskiest first, a one-line `UX target:`, and `Metrics:`
including at least one dollar-denominated loss-exposure metric (write the $).

hints.nudge: Who is this control FOR, in priority order? If your honest answer is 'the auditor', §3 calls that the disease. One owner means one name.

hints.concept: §4.1–4.2 — customers, backlog, UX, owner, metrics; §5.1 shows the exact card shape

hints.reveal: Fill the card like §5.1: 'Owner: M. Okafor', customers '1. Engineer … 2. Auditor … 3. Business …', backlog '1. 12 standing grants never expire … 2. Evidence is a manual quarterly export … 3. No alert when a grant outlives its shift', 'UX target: access auto-granted at shift start, auto-revoked at shift end; the revocation log IS the evidence', 'Metrics: standing-grant count (target 0), mean grant lifetime, evidence toil hrs/qtr, loss exposure bought down ($/yr)'.

tasks.explain:
The card didn't change the control's name — it changed what "good" means: from "the
box is checked at audit time" to a ranked backlog, an owner with a name, and a
dollar metric. The next tasks put the number on that metric; the memo's
recommendation will spend it.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 2 — read the input before you trust the output. Open `lab14/risk-input.json`
(and skim `expected_loss.ts` if you want to see exactly what will be done with it).
Then, in the memo's **Quantified loss exposure** section, state in your own words
what the two ranges mean — frequency in events/year, magnitude in dollars per
event — and why they are estimated separately (different evidence informs each).

hints.nudge: Two questions, estimated apart: how OFTEN does the loss event happen (per year), and how BAD is one occurrence (in dollars)? What different evidence would you pull for each?

hints.concept: §4.4 — the FAIR move: decompose loss into frequency and magnitude

hints.reveal: Write e.g.: 'Frequency 0.1–0.6 events/year: how often a standing grant is abused. Magnitude $300,000–$2,500,000 per event: what one incident costs. Estimated separately because different evidence informs each — incident history speaks to frequency, the value at stake speaks to magnitude.'

tasks.explain:
You can now read every field the calculator consumes — which is the difference
between quantification and a black box. A range is a real measurement (§4.3): it
has units, it combines, and it admits how uncertain you are. The red cell does none
of that.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 3 — run the reference calculator. Press **Run validator**: it computes the
loss-exposure distribution from `lab14/risk-input.json` exactly as
`bun expected_loss.ts fixtures/risk-input.json` does. Then record both figures in
the memo's **Quantified loss exposure** section: the mean expected annual loss
(the planning figure) and the 95th-percentile "bad year" (the tail).

hints.nudge: The button is the same as the command. Copy the two numbers the JSON output reports — mean and tailValue — into the memo, exactly.

hints.concept: §4.5 — sample the ranges; the distribution (mean AND tail) is the answer

hints.reveal: Run validator outputs mean 493516 and tailValue 1133873 (the §5.2 ~$494k/yr and ~$1.13M figures, unrounded). Record both in the exposure section, e.g. 'mean expected annual loss $493,516/yr; 95th-percentile bad year (the tail) $1,133,873/yr'.

tasks.explain:
The top backlog item now has a price: ~$494k/yr of expected loss with a seven-figure
tail. Because the calculator is seeded and deterministic, anyone re-running it on the
committed fixture gets these exact bytes — the quantification is reproducible
evidence, not an analyst's opinion.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 4 — move the ranges and watch the shape. Edit `lab14/risk-input.json`:
raise the magnitude maximum from 2500000 to 5000000 (the honest "what if the bad
case is twice as bad" question), then press **Run validator** again. Confirm the
distribution moved the way §4.5 predicts — wider magnitude range, fatter tail —
then add one sentence to the exposure section that names the new tail figure and
says why the tail, not the mean, is the executive's concern.

hints.nudge: Only the magnitude object's max changes — keep the JSON valid. Re-run and compare BOTH numbers to t3's: which one moved more?

hints.concept: §4.5 — the tail is the part a colored grid erases and the part executives lose sleep over

hints.reveal: Change magnitude to { "min": 300000, "max": 5000000, "unit": "USD/event" } and re-run: mean 934417, tailValue 2240391. Then write e.g.: 'The executive underwrites the bad year, not the average — doubling the worst-case magnitude moved the p95 tail to $2.24M.'

tasks.explain:
One field changed and the bad year doubled. That sensitivity is exactly what the
memo's reader needs to see — and exactly what a red/amber/green cell cannot show,
because colors have no arithmetic. Note the §4.5 caveat: uniform sampling understates
this tail, so read it as a conservative floor.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 5 — score all seven loop stages. Complete `lab14/scoring-table.tsv` in the
§5.3 shape: one tab-separated row per stage, in loop order — UNDERSTAND, LOCATE,
QUERY, EVALUATE, EVIDENCE, MONITOR, OWN — each with its deciding question and your
BUILD / BUY / HYBRID call (uppercase; the calls are the contract). The module's
one hard rule: UNDERSTAND and OWN are *always own* — context and accountability
cannot be outsourced. Every other stage is your judgment; keep a one-line reason
per call for the memo.

hints.nudge: Seven rows, one deciding question each (§4.6 gives all seven), tab-separated, calls in caps. If you scored OWN as BUY, ask: who answers the auditor when the vendor's dashboard is wrong?

hints.concept: §4.6 — the seven-stage build/buy lens, one deciding question per stage; §5.3 shows the worked table

hints.reveal: The §5.3 worked table, tab-separated: UNDERSTAND→BUILD, LOCATE→BUY, QUERY→BUY, EVALUATE→BUILD, EVIDENCE→HYBRID, MONITOR→BUY, OWN→BUILD — each row 'STAGE<tab>deciding question<tab>CALL'. Your calls on the middle five may differ; the reasons are what make them defensible.

tasks.explain:
This is the same assertion set the module's CI (`happy-path.sh`) runs against its
own lab: all seven stages present, every call a real BUILD/BUY/HYBRID token. The
reusable pattern from §5.3 — buy the breadth, own the judgment and the
accountability — emerged from the deciding questions, not from ideology.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 6 — draw the boundary line, honestly in both directions. In the memo's
**The boundary argument** section: one explicit paragraph naming which stages are
vendor-owned and which are yours, and specifically why you own (or don't) the
EVALUATE policy-and-evidence layer. Then complete BOTH lines — `Vendor wins:` with
one honest case where the platform's abstraction beats building (undifferentiated
breadth), and `Owning wins:` with one honest case where your library beats the
abstraction. For the owning case, use the module's worked one: the platform marks a
public-data server "FAIL: unencrypted disk" that you have risk-accepted with a
documented exception — the same disk-encryption claim you've chased since module 00.

hints.nudge: A boundary argued in only one direction is not a boundary — it's a posture. NIH and vendor-worship are the same mistake (§4.8): outsourcing the decision instead of making it.

hints.concept: §4.7–4.8 and §5.4 — where the abstraction pays and where owning the policy/evidence library beats it

hints.reveal: e.g. 'Vendor wins: LOCATE across forty SaaS apps — maintaining forty OAuth integrations is undifferentiated heavy lifting the platform amortizes across hundreds of customers.' 'Owning wins: the EVALUATE layer for our risk-accepted exception — the platform shows FAIL: unencrypted disk on the public-data server; our owned policy-as-code encodes the documented exception so the auditor sees a defensible decision, not a quarterly manual override.'

tasks.explain:
Both directions on file is the anti-NIH, anti-vendor-worship discipline made
structural. And notice where the laptop-encryption thread surfaced: the generic
check can read the disk flag, but only YOUR policy layer knows the exception is
documented and compensated — that nuance is precisely what the EVALUATE stage's
deciding question protects.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 7 — assemble the deliverable. Carry your seven-row scoring table (with your
one-line reasons) into the memo's **Seven-stage build/buy/hybrid scoring** section,
then close the **Recommendation** section with one paragraph that ties the boundary
to the loss number: name the dollar exposure the calculator computed, and state the
decision as a decision — which stage you own/build/buy and why that is where the
quantified risk lives. All five memo parts must now be present, in order.

verify.regex: ## Control as a product[\s\S]*## Quantified loss exposure[\s\S]*## Seven-stage build/buy/hybrid scoring[\s\S]*## The boundary argument[\s\S]*## Recommendation

hints.nudge: The §5.2 close is the template: a one-time engineering spend against a recurring $X/yr exposure with a $Y tail. A summary restates; a recommendation decides.

hints.concept: §5.2 and §5.4 — the boundary justified in the language finance accepts

hints.reveal: End with e.g.: 'We own EVALUATE (and keep UNDERSTAND/OWN) because the $493,516/yr exposure — $1,133,873 in the p95 bad year — lives in a posture the generic check cannot model; we buy LOCATE/QUERY/MONITOR as commodity breadth and run EVIDENCE hybrid. A one-time $40k time-boxing build against ~$494k/yr of recurring exposure argues itself.'

tasks.explain:
That paragraph is the whole module in one artifact: a product card that names who
it's for, a distribution instead of a color, seven deliberate calls instead of one
ideology, a boundary defended in both directions — and a recommendation a CFO can
arbitrate because it has units. This memo is the §7 assessment shape; the capstone
will ask you to produce it unaided.

tasks.instruction:
The grid demolition, in writing (4–6 sentences): a peer proposes funding either one
"high" risk closure at $200k or two "medium" closures at $50k each, using the 5×5
colored grid. Explain why the grid structurally cannot answer which to fund, how the
sampling approach you just ran answers it, and one honest limitation of OUR
calculator (§4.5's uniform-sampling caveat) that you would disclose to the executive
before they trust your tail number.

hints.nudge: Colors have no units, no zero, no interval — you cannot add two ambers or divide a red by $200k. What CAN you divide a dollar distribution by?

hints.concept: §3 and §4.5 — measurement as uncertainty reduction; the uniform-sampling tail is a conservative floor
